name: Bhaktapur
tagline: The valley's most complete medieval Newar town, 13 km from Kathmandu
meta_description: Bhaktapur guide: Durbar Square, Nyatapola temple, Pottery Square, juju dhau curd, Bisket Jatra, entry fee, how to reach from Kathmandu and where to stay.
summary: Bhaktapur is a medieval Newar town 13 km east of Kathmandu, with three brick-paved squares, the five-roof Nyatapola temple and an old centre largely closed to through traffic. A half day covers the main squares, but a night lets you see the town at dawn and dusk without the day-trip crowds.
intro: Bhaktapur, called Khwopa in the Newar language, was the capital of the whole Kathmandu Valley under the early Malla kings until the late 15th century, when the valley split into three rival kingdoms. Its wealth came from the trade route to Tibet, and it shows in the carving on every window frame and temple strut. About 80,000 people live in the municipality today, many of them farmers who still dry rice and chillies on the squares and carry loads on shoulder poles. The town feels lived in rather than preserved, and that is the reason to come.

The old town follows the line of the trade road from west to east, linking three main squares. Durbar Square holds the royal palace with its 55 Windows and the gilded Golden Gate of 1754. Taumadhi Square, a few minutes to the south-east, has the Nyatapola, at about 30 m the tallest pagoda in Nepal, built in 1702 and still standing after the earthquakes of 1934 and 2015. Dattatreya Square in the east is the oldest quarter, with woodcarving workshops and the Peacock Window. Between them run lanes of brick houses, wells and stone water spouts.

Much of what you see is careful restoration. A German-funded project from 1974 to 1986 rebuilt drains, paved lanes and repaired temples, and the municipality has used entry fees for upkeep ever since, which is why foreigners pay NPR 1,800 (about US$ 15) and SAARC and Chinese nationals NPR 500; check current status before you travel. The 2015 earthquake brought down the Vatsala Durga temple, since rebuilt, and damaged many houses. The town is busiest in mid-April for Bisket Jatra, the New Year chariot festival, and in August or September for Gai Jatra.
facts: Nyatapola temple, pottery, juju dhau curd, Bisket Jatra

highlights.title: Nyatapola and Taumadhi Square
highlights.text: Nepal's tallest pagoda rises about 30 m on five plinths, each guarded by a pair of stone figures: legendary wrestlers at the bottom, then elephants, lions, griffins and two goddesses at the top. Climb the steps at dusk and look across Taumadhi to the three-roofed Bhairavnath temple and the terrace cafés around it.

highlights.title: Durbar Square and the Golden Gate
highlights.text: The Golden Gate of 1754, gilded copper set in red brick, leads towards the palace courtyards and the Taleju temple, which only Hindus may enter. Beside it stands the Palace of 55 Windows, and across the square the rebuilt stone Vatsala Durga temple and the big Taleju bell rung at morning worship.

highlights.title: Pottery Square
highlights.text: A few minutes south of Durbar Square, potters throw pots on heavy wheels in the open, and rows of drying pots, money boxes and oil lamps cover the paving. Mornings from October to May are busiest, because the clay needs sun to dry before it is fired in kilns of straw and ash.

highlights.title: Dattatreya Square and the Peacock Window
highlights.text: The eastern square is the oldest part of town, centred on the Dattatreya temple, traditionally dated to 1427. In a lane beside the Pujari Math, a carved latticed window shows a peacock fanning its tail, the best-known single piece of Newar woodwork in the valley. Woodcarving shops line the square.

highlights.title: Juju dhau, the king of curds
highlights.text: Bhaktapur's sweet, thick curd is made from buffalo milk set overnight in unglazed clay bowls that draw out moisture and leave a firm, creamy top. Small shops near Taumadhi and Durbar Square sell it by the bowl; eat it on the spot with a wooden spoon and hand the bowl back.

highlights.title: Bisket Jatra in April
highlights.text: Nepali New Year in mid-April brings Bhaktapur's biggest festival, nine days in which the upper and lower halves of town fight a tug-of-war over the giant chariot of Bhairav in Taumadhi Square. A tall ceremonial pole is raised and then pulled down to mark the new year. Dates follow the lunar calendar; check current status before you travel.

how_to_reach.text: Bhaktapur is about 13 km east of central Kathmandu, 40 minutes to an hour by car via Koteshwor and Thimi, depending on traffic. Our private cars drop you at the western entrance near Siddha Pokhari or on the Taumadhi side. Local buses leave the Ratna Park area through the day and take about an hour; taxis cost more but save time and can wait.

Tribhuvan International Airport is only about 10 km away, a 30–45 minute transfer, so Bhaktapur works well as a first or last night. On a short trip it is a calmer base than central Kathmandu, and an evening arrival still leaves time for dinner on a terrace above Taumadhi Square.

From Changunarayan a path drops about 140 m through villages and fields to Bhaktapur in roughly 1.5–2 hours, a good way to arrive after visiting the temple. Fit walkers can also come all the way down from Nagarkot in 5–6 hours via Telkot and Changunarayan, with our car carrying the bags.

where_to_stay: We like a night inside the old town, where small family-run guesthouses occupy restored Newar brick houses around Durbar Square, Taumadhi and Dattatreya. Rooms are simple and often up steep wooden stairs, but rooftop terraces look over the pagodas and, on clear winter mornings, north to the Himalaya. Cars cannot reach most of them, so pack a bag you can carry 200–400 m along brick lanes. Travellers who want larger rooms and parking stay in modern hotels on the edge of town towards Suryabinayak or Thimi, or base themselves in Nagarkot, about 20 km up the hill, and visit Bhaktapur for the day.
tips: Keep your entry ticket for the whole visit, since staff check it at the edges of the old town, and ask at the counter whether it can be extended if you stay several days.
Arrive before 9 am or after 4 pm to see the squares at work, with farmers spreading grain and far fewer day-trip groups.
Walk clockwise around shrines and do not step over the small offerings of rice and flowers left on the paving each morning.
Buy pottery and woodcarving direct from the workshops and ask for wrapping, as small pieces survive a suitcase better than tall vases.
Wear shoes with grip, because brick paving and temple steps turn slippery after rain and in the dew of winter mornings.

experiences.title: Hands-on pottery at Bhaktapur's Pottery Square
experiences.summary: A short session with a Prajapati potter family at Pottery Square, watching clay prepared and thrown on a traditional heavy wheel, then trying the wheel yourself with the potter's hands guiding yours. You also see pots drying in the square and the straw kilns used to fire them.
body: Pottery has been a family trade in Bhaktapur for centuries, carried on mainly by the Prajapati community, whose workshops open straight onto the square a few minutes south of Durbar Square. Clay is dug from fields around the town, then soaked, trodden and kneaded by hand before it reaches the wheel. The traditional Newar wheel is a heavy disc set spinning with a stick and kept turning by its own weight, though many potters now use electric wheels for everyday production. In the morning the square fills with rows of pots, lamps, money boxes and flowerpots drying in the sun.

Our session starts with a slow walk through the square while the potter explains the process from raw clay to finished pot, including the open kilns stacked with pots, straw and ash that smoulder through the day. Then you sit at the wheel. The potter centres the clay, guides your hands to open and raise the walls, and usually rescues the result. Most people manage a small bowl or cup on the second or third try. Children over about six enjoy it, and the clay washes out of clothes easily.

Your piece needs several days to dry and fire, so it cannot leave with you the same day; if you are staying longer in the valley we can collect it, otherwise most guests buy a finished piece from the family. Prices are low, with small bowls and lamps costing a few hundred rupees. Sessions run best from October to May, as the monsoon slows drying and fewer potters work outside. Wear clothes you do not mind getting muddy, and bring some cash for the family, since tips go straight to the workshop.

faqs.q: Can children try the pottery wheel in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Yes. Children from about six upwards usually love it, and the potter keeps a hand on the wheel the whole time. Younger children can shape small pieces by hand while their parents try the wheel. Bring a change of top or an old T-shirt, since wet clay splashes, and wet wipes for the walk afterwards.

faqs.q: Can I take my pot home after the workshop?
faqs.a: Not on the same day. A freshly thrown pot needs several days to dry and then has to be fired, so it cannot go in your bag that afternoon. If you are in the valley for a few more days, we can arrange collection; otherwise buying a finished piece from the same family is the usual answer.

faqs.q: Do I need a Bhaktapur entry ticket to visit Pottery Square?
faqs.a: Yes, for foreign and SAARC visitors, because Pottery Square lies inside the ticketed old town. Foreigners pay NPR 1,800 and SAARC and Chinese nationals NPR 500, and the same ticket covers Durbar, Taumadhi and Dattatreya squares. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Durbar Square, Taumadhi and Dattatreya walk
experiences.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, all year
experiences.summary: A three-hour guided walk joining Bhaktapur's three royal and temple squares along the old trade road, from the Golden Gate and Palace of 55 Windows to the Nyatapola pagoda and on to Dattatreya Square, with stops at water spouts, courtyards and workshops along the way.
body: We enter from the west near Siddha Pokhari, a large rectangular water tank from the Malla period, and follow the main lane into Durbar Square. Your guide explains how the palace grew under King Bhupatindra Malla around 1700 and points out the Golden Gate, the Palace of 55 Windows, the Vatsala Durga temple and the bronze statue of Bhupatindra Malla himself, seated on a tall pillar facing the palace. The National Art Gallery, in one wing of the palace, has fine paubha paintings and old manuscripts if you want to add an hour.

From Durbar Square a lane of carvers' shops leads a few minutes south-east to Taumadhi Square. The Nyatapola, built in 1702 on five plinths, is the tallest pagoda in Nepal at about 30 m. Facing it is the Bhairavnath temple, whose chariot is the centre of Bisket Jatra in April. On the way we look into a working Newar courtyard and a sunken stone water spout, or hiti, where families still fill pots and wash in the mornings. Pottery Square is a short detour if you want it.

The last stretch follows the old main road east, past shrines, small dye shops and studios painting thangkas, to Dattatreya Square. This is where Bhaktapur began, and its three-roofed Dattatreya temple is traditionally dated to 1427. Beside the square, the Pujari Math houses a woodcarving museum, with the Peacock Window set in its outer wall. We finish here with tea or a bowl of juju dhau. The walk covers about 2 km on brick paving with a few temple steps, and suits most ages at a gentle pace.

faqs.q: How much time do you need in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Three to four hours covers the three squares and Pottery Square at a comfortable pace, which is how most day trips from Kathmandu work. Stay overnight if you can: early morning and dusk are the best times for photographs, the squares are quieter, and you can add the National Art Gallery, the woodcarving museum and a food trail without rushing.

faqs.q: What is the Bhaktapur entry fee for Indians?
faqs.a: Indian visitors pay the SAARC rate of NPR 500 (about ₹310), against NPR 1,800 for most other foreigners, while Nepali citizens enter free. Carry a passport or voter ID in case staff ask for proof of nationality at the ticket booth. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Bhaktapur Durbar Square still damaged from the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Most of it has been repaired. The 2015 earthquake brought down the Vatsala Durga temple and damaged palace wings and many houses, while the Nyatapola survived intact. Vatsala Durga has since been rebuilt, and restoration continues on a few buildings, so you may still see scaffolding in places.

experiences.title: Juju dhau and Newar snacks food trail
experiences.summary: A two-hour tasting walk through Bhaktapur's lanes for the dishes the town is known for: juju dhau curd in clay bowls, wo lentil patties, chatamari, the samay baji festival plate and spiced kachila, with a guide who explains when and why Newar families eat each one.
body: Bhaktapur's food is built on what its farming families grow and the buffalo they keep. Our trail starts at about 4 pm near Taumadhi Square with wo, the local Newar name for bara: black-lentil batter fried flat on an iron pan and eaten hot from a leaf. From there we work through the lanes towards Durbar Square, stopping at small family kitchens with low benches and a single pan over the flame. Each stop is a tasting rather than a meal, so you can pace yourself across five or six places.

Next comes chatamari, a thin rice-flour pancake topped with minced meat or egg, followed by samay baji, the festival plate of beaten rice, roasted soybeans, fresh ginger, potato achar and boiled egg. Meat eaters can try kachila, minced buffalo marinated raw with mustard oil, ginger and spices, a Newar speciality that is an acquired taste and best skipped if your stomach is new to Nepal. Vegetarians are well looked after with potato and soybean dishes, meatless chatamari and fresh sweets from the market stalls.

The finale is juju dhau, the king of curds. Buffalo milk is boiled, sweetened and left to set overnight in unglazed clay bowls, making a curd thicker and creamier than ordinary dahi, and the Bhaktapur version is the one Nepalis carry home as a gift. We stop at a long-running shop where you eat a small bowl on the spot and can buy a sealed one for your hotel. Allow two hours, come hungry, and bring small notes for any extra snacks you want to buy along the way.

faqs.q: What is juju dhau and why is Bhaktapur famous for it?
faqs.a: Juju dhau means king of curds in Newari. It is a sweet, thick curd made from buffalo milk and set overnight in porous clay bowls that draw out water, giving a firm, creamy texture. Bhaktapur's shops have made it for generations, and Nepalis visiting the town often take a bowl home as a gift.

faqs.q: Is the Bhaktapur food trail okay for vegetarians?
faqs.a: Yes. Vegetarians can eat wo, chatamari without meat, the potato and soybean parts of the samay baji plate and juju dhau, which together make a filling trail. Tell us when you book and the guide will choose kitchens that keep meat separate. Strict Jain diets are harder, because onion and garlic go into most savoury dishes.

faqs.q: Can I carry juju dhau back to Kathmandu or India?
faqs.a: To Kathmandu, yes: a sealed clay bowl keeps for a day or so in cool weather if you carry it upright. Taking it on a flight is harder, because curd counts as a liquid or gel in hand luggage and may be refused at security. Eat it in Nepal and buy pottery as your souvenir instead.

faqs.q: Is Bhaktapur worth visiting if I have already seen Kathmandu Durbar Square?
faqs.a: Yes. Bhaktapur is larger, quieter and better restored than Kathmandu's square, with cars kept out of most of the old town, so you see a whole Newar town rather than a single monument zone. Its pottery, woodcarving and food culture are distinct too. If you only have time for one of the valley's three Durbar Squares, many travellers choose Bhaktapur.

faqs.q: How far is Bhaktapur from Kathmandu and how do I get there?
faqs.a: Bhaktapur is about 13 km east of central Kathmandu, 40 minutes to an hour by car depending on traffic. A private car with driver for a half day is the easiest option. Local buses from the Ratna Park area take about an hour, and taxis cost roughly NPR 1,200–1,800 each way; check current rates before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the Bhaktapur entry fee?
faqs.a: Foreigners pay NPR 1,800 (about US$ 15) and SAARC and Chinese nationals NPR 500 to enter the old town, while Nepali citizens enter free. Tickets are sold at booths on the main approaches and checked at several points inside. Fees are revised from time to time, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Should I stay overnight in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: If your schedule allows, yes. Day-trip groups arrive from about 10 am and leave by 4 pm, so evenings and early mornings belong to residents, temple bells and farmers drying grain on the squares. A night in a guesthouse also lets you watch sunrise over the Himalaya from a rooftop on clear days between October and February.

faqs.q: When is Bisket Jatra in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Bisket Jatra falls around Nepali New Year in mid-April and usually lasts nine days, with the chariot of Bhairav hauled through Taumadhi Square and a tall pole raised and toppled to mark the new year. Exact dates follow the lunar calendar, and the square gets crowded and rough during chariot pulling, so book early and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What can I buy in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Pottery from Pottery Square, woodcarvings and small copies of the Peacock Window from Dattatreya Square, thangka paintings, handmade lokta paper and the black cotton cloth with a red border known as haku patasi. Prices are fair compared with Thamel, and buying from workshops means the money reaches the makers. Ask for wrapping before you pack.

faqs.q: Is Bhaktapur good for families with children?
faqs.a: Very good. Most of the old town is car-free, the squares are open, and the pottery wheel, pigeons, water spouts and juju dhau keep children interested. The brick lanes are uneven for prams, so a baby carrier works better. Plan breaks at the terrace cafés above Taumadhi Square, where children can watch the square from a safe height.

faqs.q: What is the best time of day to photograph Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Early morning, from sunrise to about 9 am, and the last two hours before sunset. Low light picks out the carving on the Nyatapola and the palace windows, and the squares fill with residents rather than tour groups. Midday light from March to May is flat and hazy. Drones need prior government permission; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can I combine Bhaktapur with Nagarkot or Changunarayan?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a natural pairing. Changunarayan is about 6 km north of Bhaktapur and Nagarkot about 20 km north-east, so a popular plan is Bhaktapur in the afternoon, a night in Nagarkot for sunrise, then the walk down to Changunarayan. Our private car follows to carry the bags and pick you up at the end.
